passage: The night train between Averil and the coast will run again from December, nine years after the sleeper service was withdrawn, the regional rail authority announced on Tuesday. The revived service will leave Averil at 10:55 p.m. on Thursdays, Fridays, and Sundays, arriving at the harbor station at 6:10 a.m., with a stop at Combe Junction added after lobbying from the three ski villages served by its branch line. Fares start at 39 dollars for a reclining seat and 89 dollars for a berth in a shared twin cabin. The authority has leased four refurbished sleeping cars from a museum trust, an arrangement critics called fragile, since the cars date from 1968 and spare parts must be machined to order. A spokesman answered that the trust's workshop has kept the cars running on excursions for two decades and holds drawings for every component. The service needs to sell about 60 percent of its berths to break even, a target the old service missed in its final three years. Bookings open on the first of October, and the authority says the first four weekends are already half reserved by tour operators.
question: At what time will the night train leave Averil?

passage: A homemade raft made of 44 sealed barrels and a garden shed took first place in Sunday's Brackwater river race, completing the two mile course in 58 minutes despite losing part of its roof to a low bridge. The crew of six, calling themselves the Shedheads, beat 23 other rafts and collected the silver oar trophy along with 400 dollars for the lifeboat fund, the race's designated charity, which took in 9,200 dollars overall from entry fees and bankside collections. Second place went to a pedal powered platform from the rowing club, three minutes back, and the prize for best costume went to a crew dressed as chess pieces whose raft, a checkerboard of painted pallets, sank gently and completely within sight of the finish; all eight were pulled out by the safety boats to the loudest cheer of the day. Organizers reported one twisted ankle and one lost wedding ring, later found inside a bailing bucket. The race, run since 1977, was cancelled only once, for high water in 2000. Next year's edition falls on the last Sunday of July, and the Shedheads say they will defend their title with a taller shed.
question: How long did the winning raft take to complete the course?

passage: The county's bookmobile, a familiar green van that has served the hill villages for 26 years, made its final rounds on Friday and will be replaced by two smaller electric vans beginning next month. The old van, which needed a costly gearbox rebuild to pass inspection, logged just over 400,000 miles in service and carried, at the end, about 2,800 books, along with a printer for library cards and a wheelchair lift added in 2009. The new vans carry 1,600 books each but will double the number of stops, adding fourteen new ones, including the caravan site at Lower Fern and the veterans home on Aldous Hill, both of which had petitioned for service for years. Chief librarian Rowan Delacroix-Mbeki said the electric vans charge overnight at the depot and manage the steepest route, the Wintergreen loop, with about 30 percent of charge to spare in trials. The old van will not be scrapped: a collective of puppeteers has bought it for a traveling theater, promising to keep the green paint. Regular riders gathered at the last stop with a sheet cake iced to look like a library card.
question: How many new stops will the two electric vans add?

passage: An escaped flock of 60 sheep delayed the morning's first flight out of Marden regional airport on Thursday, after the animals pushed through a fence panel bent by Tuesday's windstorm and spread across the grass margins of the single runway. Ground staff spotted the flock at 5:40 a.m., about an hour before the scheduled 6:45 departure to the capital, and the airport's wildlife officer decided against using the siren, which she judged would scatter the sheep in all directions including onto the paved surface. Instead the farmer, reached at home, arrived with two dogs, and the flock was folded back through the gap and penned in the airport's own equipment yard within forty minutes. The flight left 55 minutes late with all 48 passengers. The airport manager, Bram Toussaint, said the fence line had been walked after the storm but the bent panel, hidden behind a fuel shed, was missed, and that the entire western fence will now be renewed early, a job budgeted at 130,000 dollars for next year. It was the airport's first animal incursion since a swan in 2018. The sheep were returned home by trailer before noon, none injured.
question: How late did the delayed flight leave?

passage: The old cinema on Grafton Parade, dark since 2014, will reopen next spring as a three screen house run by a community trust that raised the purchase price in fourteen months of fundraising. The trust paid 620,000 dollars for the building, aided by a heritage grant of 200,000 dollars tied to restoring the 1938 facade and its neon sign, which will be recreated by the same family firm that maintained the original until the 1980s. Inside, the single 700 seat auditorium will be divided into rooms of 300, 120, and 60 seats, with the largest keeping the ornate plaster ceiling and the balcony rail. The trust sold 2,100 community shares at 100 dollars each and reports 380 volunteers on its register, from projectionists to painters. Programming will mix new releases with a Wednesday classics night and a monthly subtitled screening for deaf audiences. Trust chair Golda Pereira said the cinema must sell about 1,100 tickets a week to cover costs, a figure the old operator managed until a multiplex opened on the ring road. That multiplex closed itself last winter, leaving the town of 40,000 with no cinema at all.
question: How much did the trust pay for the cinema building?

passage: Divers surveying the wreck of the collier Maud Ellen, sunk in a storm in 1908, have recovered the ship's bell from 90 feet of water and confirmed the identity of a wreck that generations of local fishermen simply called the coal boat. The bell, raised under permit and now in conservation, carries the vessel's name and the year 1891, when she was launched from a yard that built more than 200 such ships before closing in 1921. The survey team, twelve volunteers working from an inflatable over six weekends, mapped the wreck with tape measures and cameras, producing a plan that shows the hull broken in two at the boiler room, consistent with newspaper accounts of the sinking that describe her going down in minutes after her cargo shifted. All fourteen of her crew were lost; nine are buried in the churchyard at Skerne, where the recovered bell will eventually hang in a memorial garden approved by the parish last year. Team leader Aldo Brennan said the group will not raise anything further, and has asked anglers to avoid anchoring on the site, which now has provisional protection while the heritage office considers a permanent order.
question: In what year was the Maud Ellen launched?

passage: The regional science fair's top award went on Saturday to a fifteen year old who spent two years measuring how street lighting changes the singing times of blackbirds, a project the judges praised for its patience and its plain methods. Working before school, Tam Rachlin logged first song at 46 sites across her town, pairing each lit site with a darker one of similar tree cover, and found birds at the brightest sites began singing on average 43 minutes earlier, with the gap widening in winter. Her equipment amounted to a bicycle, a voice recorder, and a light meter borrowed from the school's photography club. The fair drew 214 entries from 31 schools; runner-up prizes went to a study of rust on three bridge alloys and to a working model of a tidal sluice. Rachlin's project also won the ornithology society's junior medal, which carries 250 dollars and a year's membership. Asked about next steps, she said she wants to repeat the survey after the town finishes converting its 5,600 streetlights to dimmable ones, a program set to end next autumn, to see whether the birds shift back.
question: How much earlier on average did birds at the brightest sites begin singing?

passage: A water tower that has loomed over the rail yards since 1912 was lowered to the ground in one piece on Sunday, the centerpiece of a delicate six hour operation watched by a crowd that police estimated at 2,000. The 70 ton riveted tank, empty since 1967, was lifted from its legs by the largest crane ever brought into the town, an 800 ton machine that arrived in 14 truckloads and took three days to assemble. The tank will be restored over winter and re-erected in the spring at the railway museum two miles away, where it will stand beside the roundhouse on new legs fabricated to the original 1912 drawings, the originals being too corroded to certify. The move costs 380,000 dollars, met by the museum's foundation and a state transport heritage fund. One anxious moment came at 9:20 a.m., when a lifting lug groaned loudly enough to pause the operation; engineers inspected it for forty minutes before resuming. The tank touched down on its transport cradle at 1:15 p.m. to applause. The museum expects the reassembled tower to open with a viewing platform inside the tank itself.
question: How much does the water tower move cost?

passage: The shellfish beds at Gorman Flats will reopen on Monday for the first time in 20 months, the marine authority announced, after twelve consecutive water samples met the safety standard for the bacteria that closed the fishery. The closure, imposed after heavy rains overwhelmed the Millhaven sewage works in two successive winters, idled 34 licensed gatherers and shut the flats' small packing shed, which in a normal year handles about 90 tons of clams. The works has since been fitted with a storm storage tank of 4 million gallons, finished in March at a cost of 11 million dollars, and the authority credits the tank with the clean samples, noting that two heavy storms since March produced no measurable spike on the flats. Gatherers will face a reduced quota for the first season, 60 percent of the pre-closure allowance, while the beds are assessed, and the authority will sample weekly rather than monthly for at least a year. The gatherers association, which had pressed a compensation claim against the water company, said the claim continues regardless of reopening; it seeks 1.9 million dollars for lost seasons.
question: How many licensed gatherers were idled by the closure?

passage: A first edition atlas missing from the Corvin college library for over forty years has been returned by mail, wrapped in brown paper and accompanied by an unsigned note of apology. The parcel, postmarked from a city 600 miles away, arrived on a Tuesday and was opened by an assistant who recognized the library's old bookplate at once. The atlas, printed in 1734 and containing 42 hand colored maps, vanished sometime between a 1979 inventory and the next full count in 1983; the library long assumed it had been stolen during a chaotic building move in 1981. The note says only that the sender found the volume among a late relative's belongings and that the relative had spoken of borrowing it and never daring to return it. Conservators report the book in remarkably good condition, kept dry and out of light, with one map, the double page chart of the western isles, showing a repaired tear that was not recorded in 1979. The library will not pursue any inquiry, its director said, calling the return the best possible ending. The atlas goes on display in the entrance hall case for one month before returning to the vault.
question: How many hand colored maps does the atlas contain?
